original_question: Does every planar graph have obstacle number 1?
target_in_paper: Section 2.5, Open Problem 11: "Does every planar graph have obstacle number 1?"
correct_elements: Your draft matches the paper’s intended target essentially verbatim. It identifies the right object class (planar graphs) and the right parameter (obstacle number), and it asks exactly the same yes/no question posed as Open Problem 11 in Section 2.5.
missing_details: The paper defines obstacle number only after defining an obstacle representation, so the question is not fully stand-alone unless that definition is unpacked.
In this paper, an obstacle representation uses a set of points in the plane for the vertices together with a set of simple polygonal obstacles in the plane.
Two represented vertices are adjacent exactly when the straight-line segment joining their points does not intersect any obstacle.
The section assumes a general-position condition: the segment joining any two vertex-points does not pass through another vertex-point or through a vertex of an obstacle.
To make the question fully self-contained, one should say finite simple planar graph G rather than just planar graph.
The paper’s version is the standard obstacle-number notion from Section 2.5; it is not the convex-obstacle, outside-obstacle, grid-obstacle, or plane-graph variant.
refined_question: For every finite simple planar graph G, is the obstacle number of G equal to 1; that is, does G admit an obstacle representation in the Euclidean plane with a single simple polygonal obstacle, where the vertices of G are represented by points and uv is an edge of G if and only if the straight-line segment joining the points for u and v avoids the obstacle, under the general-position assumption used in Section 2.5 that such segments pass through neither other vertex-points nor obstacle vertices?
justification: This is the exact open problem your draft is trying to capture, not a broader neighboring one. Section 2.5 first introduces obstacle representations and defines the obstacle number of a graph, then lists Open Problems 8–11; Open Problem 11 is precisely the question in your draft. The only necessary refinement is to make the question self-contained by spelling out the paper’s definition of obstacle number and its implicit geometric assumptions, while avoiding later variants of obstacle representations that are not the target here.
